text.text: Run the company from here. A survey becomes an estimate, a deposit books the date, and the Moves board shows every crew and truck on the calendar. Mark done stamps the finish; the final bill goes out the same day. Damage claims keeps every reported scratch until it is settled. Sent and overdue invoices both count in Awaiting payment.

Rename trucks and move types, set your own hourly rates, and delete the sample customers once a dozen of your own are in. Type in any cell or drag cards between columns; every total updates by itself.

Most local moves are billed by the hour from arrival to the end of unloading, plus travel and materials. The estimate on the move is what you told the customer; the final bill uses the real hours. When the two are far apart, look at the survey: missed rooms, stairs or a long carry are the usual causes.
Moves by status, revenue by type of move and unpaid invoices.
Most bad moves start with a bad estimate. Ten minutes on a video call or a walk-through saves hours of arguing on move day.
Add the customer and a move as
Ask the move date, how flexible it is, and whether the new place is ready (closing dates slip).
Book a walk-through or a video survey with the move coordinator.
What to look at, room by room
Every room, closets, garage, basement, attic and shed; open the closets
Big and awkward items: pianos, safes, gym equipment, glass tabletops, TVs without boxes
What is not going: mark it now so the crew does not load it
Who packs: the customer, or our crew for some or all rooms
at both ends: stairs, elevators (book them), long carries, parking for a 26 ft truck, loading docks
: a 1-bedroom is usually two movers and a 16 ft truck; a 3-bedroom house four movers and a 26 ft truck.
Estimate hours: loading, drive, unloading, plus time for stairs and long carries. Add the travel charge from the yard.
goes up with crew size. Write the minimum (most companies use three hours).
Packing materials: count boxes per room; a 3-bedroom house often needs 80 to 120 boxes.
Put the estimate and the costs on the move. Under 20 percent margin shows as Thin.
What the customer gets in writing
Rate, minimum hours, travel charge, and what happens if it runs over
Coverage: basic coverage pays by weight; full value costs extra. Ask which they want.

; the Dashboard lists booked moves with no deposit so the office can chase them.

A couple in a 2-bedroom townhouse wants to move on a Friday. On the video survey the coordinator sees a narrow stair turn, a sleeper sofa and 40 boxes of books. She books three movers and a 20 ft truck for seven hours, adds a packing day for the kitchen, and explains that the sofa may need its legs off. They pay the deposit that night.
Move day is a performance the customer watches all day. Arrive on time, protect the house, explain before you do, and leave nothing behind.
The coordinator confirms the time, addresses, elevator bookings and parking with the customer.
The crew lead checks the truck: fuel, pads, dollies, straps, tool kit, floor runners, door jamb covers, mattress bags.
Introduce the crew; walk the house with the customer
Agree what goes, what stays, and what is fragile or valuable (jewelry, documents and medicines travel with the customer)
Note existing damage to furniture and walls, with photos
Floor runners and door jamb covers down before the first item moves
Start the clock and tell the customer the start time
Heavy and square items first (dressers, appliances), then furniture, then boxes, then fragile pieces on top.
Pad and wrap every piece of wooden furniture; mattresses in bags.
Tie off every tier with straps.
Disassemble only what must be disassembled; bag and label all screws.
Ask where each large piece goes before carrying it in.
A final walk with the customer through both houses and the empty truck.
Stop the clock, add travel and materials, and go through the bill with the customer.
Take payment, or mark the invoice
Ask the customer to look over their things and report damage within the time your terms allow.

A senior downsizing move: the crew lead walks the house with the customer and her daughter and labels every piece that goes to assisted living with blue tape. Everything else goes to the daughter's garage on a second stop. At the new room the crew hangs pictures and makes the bed. The daughter writes a review that night.
If the move is running past the estimate, the crew lead tells the customer by the halfway point, with a new estimate, never at the end.
Even careful crews damage something now and then. How you handle it decides whether you get a referral or a one-star review.
Thank them and take it seriously. Ask for photos and when they noticed.
, and what the customer says happened.
Check the move's arrival photos. Existing damage noted on the day is not a claim.
Tell the customer what happens next and when: a call within two working days.
Ask the crew lead what they remember. Most crews will tell you honestly.
and look at the item, or have a repairer look.
Repair first where you can. A good furniture repairer fixes most scratches and dents for far less than replacement, and customers are usually happier.
pays a set amount per pound, which is small. Explain it kindly: it was on the estimate they signed.

Every month, look at the claims list with the crew leads. Two dents in the same narrow hallway type means more door jamb and corner protection. Several lamp bases means a better way of packing them. Never punish a crew member for reporting damage; punish hiding it.

A customer reports a cracked lamp base two days after a downsizing move. The crew lead remembers the box was packed by the customer. The office explains basic coverage, offers a goodwill amount, and the customer accepts. The claim is marked Paid out, and the team agrees to offer to repack fragile boxes packed by customers.
